criteria.text: Given the Command Center, when it is opened, then every tab is reachable and every card drills down one level.
Given sample mode, when any tab is shown, then the sample data is visibly labelled as sample.

Given the Command Center, when any tab renders, then .colaberry/plan.json and .colaberry/progress.json are both committed in this repo and every tab reads its content from them at runtime rather than from hard-coded values.
Given the Command Center, when any tab is shown, then .colaberry/manifest.json is committed in this repo and every tab shows how old that data is and warns when the age exceeds a week.
Trust — no tab shows a number, a connection or a result the project has not actually produced.
Given a new user, when they create a vault, then a recovery key is generated.
Given a user with a vault, when they attempt to create another vault, then they are prompted to use the existing vault.
Trust: The recovery key is securely generated and stored only on the user's device.

stories.notes: CLI demo (Sifra.Cli) prints the recovery key once on first run and the existing-vault message on second run; verified manually against an isolated temp APPDATA. Recovery key: 160-bit RandomNumberGenerator output, Base32-encoded; only a PBKDF2-SHA256 (210k iterations) hash of it is persisted, never the plaintext.

criteria.text: Given a user is logged in, when they add a new credential, then it should appear in the list.
Given a user is viewing a credential, when they choose to copy the username or password, then it should be copied to the clipboard.
Trust: All actions are logged with a timestamp and user ID.

stories.notes: Username and password are encrypted at rest (AES-GCM, key derived via PBKDF2 from the same vault credential STORY-013 uses, but a separate persisted salt so the two derived outputs are cryptographically independent) — a deliberate, user-approved decision to go beyond this story's literal brief rather than ship plaintext secrets. Label and Url are kept as plaintext metadata (documented scoping choice, not yet confirmed with user). Added first external dependency: TextCopy (cross-platform clipboard) — flagged to user, encryption choice explicitly confirmed, clipboard package usage implicitly accepted pending final confirmation. CredentialService does not itself enforce authentication — callers (CLI demo, tests) pass the same vault credential already proven via VaultAuthenticator; a real session/lock gate is STORY-004/005's job. Reuses the existing AuditLogger (STORY-015) without modification; verified no plaintext secret ever appears in log lines.

criteria.text: Given a user is logged into the vault, when they request a new password, then a strong password is generated.
Given a user requests a password of specific length, when the length is invalid, then an error message is displayed.
Trust: Generated passwords are logged with a timestamp for audit purposes.

stories.notes: Deliberate deviation from the literal acceptance text: the audit log records that a password was generated (timestamp, user, requested length) but never the password value itself — logging real secrets would violate the no-secrets-in-logs rule that governs this whole project. Reused AuditLogger (STORY-015) unmodified. PasswordGenerator does not itself enforce authentication (same convention as STORY-002 — a real session/lock gate is STORY-004/005's job). Length bounds are [8, 128]; strength is guaranteed inclusion of lowercase/uppercase/digit/symbol via a crypto-random Fisher-Yates shuffle, using RandomNumberGenerator.GetInt32 (BCL, already unbiased).

criteria.text: Given a user has locked the vault, when they unlock it, then all credentials should be accessible.
Given a user closes the application, when they reopen it, then the vault should be in a locked state.
Trust: Vault data is encrypted and persists without loss on close/reopen.

stories.notes: VaultSession is a new, self-contained layer that reuses VaultAuthenticator (STORY-013) and bridges to CredentialService (STORY-002) via RequireUnlockedCredential() without modifying either file. A fresh session always starts Locked by construction — this is structural (new in-memory object), not a persisted flag, since unlocked state is runtime-only and should never be written to disk. Known hardening gap, documented in code: the unlocked credential is held as a plain string for the session's lifetime because CredentialService's API takes the credential as a string per call; .NET strings cannot be reliably zeroed from memory. Moving to derived key material would require changing CredentialService's signature — left for a future hardening pass. "Data corruption" failure path reuses STORY-002's VaultDecryptionFailedException (AES-GCM auth-tag check) rather than adding new corruption-handling code. "Crash during unlock" is modeled as an exception interrupting the read Unlock() depends on; Unlock() performs no writes, so a real crash there cannot corrupt persisted data.

criteria.text: Given a user is logged in, when they change their master password, then the password is updated successfully.
Given a user enters an incorrect current password, when attempting to change it, then an error message is displayed.
Trust: Password change events are logged with user ID and timestamp.

stories.notes: IMPORTANT — retroactive fix to STORY-002: VaultEncryptionService.DeriveKey previously derived the encryption key directly from the vault credential via PBKDF2, which made REQ-008 impossible (changing the password would have made every existing credential permanently undecryptable). Fixed by switching to envelope encryption: a persistent random vault master key (VMK) is wrapped under a password-derived key-encryption-key (KEK); changing the password re-wraps the VMK without touching any credential ciphertext. VaultEncryptionService.DeriveKey/Encrypt/Decrypt public signatures are unchanged, so CredentialService and VaultSession needed zero code changes. Extracted the AES-GCM primitive into AesGcmCipher to avoid duplicating it for key-wrapping; deleted the now-dead VaultEncryptionKeyStore/VaultEncryptionSaltRecord. Updated one STORY-002 test whose assumption was exactly the bug (deriving with a wrong password now fails immediately, not silently). Also fixed an unrelated pre-existing flaky test in VaultSessionTests.cs (corruption via global string replace could miss the target character depending on random ciphertext bytes). Confirmed via test: raw credentials.json is byte-for-byte identical before and after a password change. MasterPasswordService reuses VaultAuthenticator.SetCredential (STORY-013) and AuditLogger (STORY-015) unmodified. Caveat documented in code: a VaultSession already unlocked with the old password becomes stale after a change and must be re-locked/unlocked; not enforced automatically since that would require touching VaultSession.cs (STORY-004).

criteria.text: Given a user has a valid recovery key, when they use it, then access to the vault is restored.
Given a user enters an invalid recovery key, when attempting recovery, then an error message is displayed.
Trust: Recovery attempts are logged with user ID and timestamp.

stories.notes: Deep architectural extension, agreed with user upfront (same class of gap as STORY-005, one layer further): recovery must restore real access to existing credentials, not just reset the login check. VaultMasterKeyStore/VaultEncryptionService extended from a single wrapped key to named multi-slot envelope encryption (master-password and recovery-key slots both wrap the same VMK). Traced to a real STORY-001 gap: CreateVault() never captured an initial master password, so the two slots cannot both be seeded at vault-creation time in one step -- VaultRecoveryService.EstablishRecoverySlot() bridges this by creating the master-password slot (bootstrapping the VMK) and then wrapping the same VMK under the recovery key, called once right after CreateVault() while the recovery key plaintext is available. VaultService gained additive VerifyRecoveryKey/IsRecoveryKeyConsumed/ConsumeRecoveryKey methods (no existing method changed) and VaultRecord gained a backward-compatible nullable RecoveryKeyConsumedAtUtc field. Recovery key is single-use (matches the original STORY-000 data model: consumed on recovery) -- expired is modeled as already used since there is no time-based expiry concept in this vault. Confirmed via test: credentials.json is untouched by recovery, and an existing credential added before recovery is still readable under the new password after recovery, even after an intervening STORY-005 password change (both slots independently wrap the same VMK). Full existing 66-test suite re-verified unaffected by the multi-slot schema change before adding anything new.

criteria.text: Given a user is logged into cloud storage, when they access the vault, then they must authenticate separately for the vault.
Given a user logs out of cloud storage, when they access the vault, then they must authenticate for the vault.
Trust: Vault access is logged independently of cloud storage access.

stories.notes: Vault authentication (VaultAuthenticator/VaultAccessCredentialStore) has no reference to ICloudAuthProvider or any cloud state — structural separation, not just tested behavior. Cloud auth modeled behind ICloudAuthProvider with a local fake (LocalFakeCloudAuthProvider) since no real cloud provider is integrated yet (that is STORY-007); swapping in a real provider later requires no change to vault auth code. Vault and cloud access are logged to two separate files (vault-access.log / cloud-access.log), not a shared log with a tag.

criteria.text: Given a user is offline, when they access the vault, then they should be able to view and edit credentials.
Given a user makes changes offline, when they reconnect, then changes should sync with the cloud.
Trust: Offline changes are logged and queued for sync.

stories.notes: CAVEAT — REVISIT AFTER STORY-002 AND STORY-007: criteria 1 and 2 are ticked against a placeholder VaultDataItem (not the real Credential model from STORY-002) and a LocalFakeCloudSyncProvider (not real Google Drive/OneDrive/Dropbox sync from STORY-007). Both were unbuilt at the time this story was completed, and the portal gates r1 (which includes STORY-002/007) behind this story and STORY-015, so ticking here was a deliberate, agreed call to unblock the build rather than leaving the project stuck. The underlying mechanism (VaultDataStore, OfflineChangeQueueStore, ICloudSyncProvider seam, VaultDataService) is real and durable — swapping in the real Credential type and a real cloud provider later should be a same-shape replacement, not a rewrite. When STORY-002 and STORY-007 land, re-verify these two criteria against the real types and re-tick with genuine evidence if anything differs.

criteria.text: Given any vault operation occurs, when the operation is completed, then it is logged with a timestamp and user ID.
Given a logging failure occurs, when an operation is attempted, then the system retries logging and alerts the admin.
Trust: All operations are logged with a unique operation ID for traceability.

stories.notes: Additive wiring: VaultService, VaultAuthenticator and VaultDataService each take an optional AuditLogger (default null = no-op), so STORY-001/013/014 behavior and their existing tests are unaffected when no logger is passed (confirmed: all prior tests still pass). UserId is Environment.UserName — this app has no account/identity system, so the OS user is the honest identifier available today. Admin alerting uses IAdminAlertSink + LocalFakeAdminAlertSink, a stand-in for a real channel (email/Slack/etc.) since no such integration or credentials exist yet. Credentials/passwords are never included in log details (verified by test).
